title: Looking Beyond the Leaders: A Mid-Year Perspective on Global Equities
summary: Despite geopolitical uncertainty and market volatility, global equities continue to offer opportunities beyond the narrow group of stocks driving index returns. - 9 min read
body_text: Markets & Economy Looking Beyond the Leaders: A Mid-Year Perspective on Global Equities Matt Burdett Head of Equities, Portfolio Manager and Managing Director 22 Jul 2026 9 min read Despite geopolitical uncertainty and market volatility, global equities continue to offer opportunities beyond the narrow group of stocks driving index returns. After six months of surprises in 2026, many themes we have highlighted over the last 18 months remain equally topical today: The tensions between politics and economic resilience Whether uncertainty is appropriately priced into various asset classes and regional markets The capital intensity of the race in artificial intelligence Balancing the search for yield against being fairly compensated for risk As was the case six months ago (and a year ago), we enter the back half of 2026 with limited clarity on the trajectory for the global economy or capital markets. After digesting the evolving U.S. tariff regime and conflict in the Middle East, thus far we’ve seen surprising resilience across most of the global economy. But global equity markets have narrowed considerably in recent years, particularly in the U.S. The second quarter saw a further dramatic reduction in breadth as AI-related stocks garnered most of the attention following the initial ceasefire agreement between the U.S. and Iran. One surprising observation was that the S&P 500’s rally in 2Q26 ranked as the fourth-largest quarterly advance in history. An important nuance is that the three biggest moves came when markets bounced off the bottom following the Global Financial Crisis and peak COVID, while last quarter was simply a move off already reasonably high levels. With the current market (especially in the U.S.) oriented around momentum and mega-cap beta, it is essential to remain focused on individual security analysis and downside protection while pursuing differentiated returns. The following observations highlight key considerations from our diverse global equity investment team while offering a differentiated perspective rooted in active management. A Resilient Global Economy Trade uncertainty was high as the Trump administration unveiled, negotiated, reversed, and re-applied a variety of tariffs over the last 15 months. The outcome? Globalization, which extends beyond trade with the U.S., has continued largely unabated. Gross exports grew across the world’s major economies, even as some supply chains were modestly reorganized in relation to the U.S. Most economies outside the U.S. remain on stable footing despite tariff-related economic friction, providing a still-solid backdrop for healthy corporate earnings around the world. Global Trade Growth Has Continued Despite Tariff Friction Gross Exports 12 Months Before and After Liberation Day ($ Trillions) Source: Bloomberg, as of 31 March 2026 Before is April 2024 – March 2025 (representing the year before Trump’s tariffs/Liberation Day) After is April 2025 – March 2026 (representing the year after tariffs started) Prior to the Iran conflict, the resilience of global economies to withstand trade frictions had indicated we could have a solid environment for stock selection to shine, and this proved to be the case in January and February. But closure of the Strait of Hormuz elevated tail risks, and we’ve seen a narrower market – first in March with risk-off trading, and then the semiconductor-led AI rally of the second quarter. Uncertainty is again higher with the collapse of the ceasefire, but the good news is that commodity price declines in June demonstrated that if that if commercial players and market participants expect the Strait of Hormuz to be even partially open, many key inputs and indicators of economic health can return to levels they’d been at 6-9 months prior to March. This contrasts from disruptions when Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, and many dislocations did not normalize for at least 12 months. Key Economic Indicators Have Normalized More Quickly than Prior Energy Shocks Source: Bloomberg, as of 20 July 2026 While the continuation of growth trends in the rest of the world is now better protected with energy prices lower than during March, and interest rates and currencies remaining reasonably stable, there is a divergence between macro and micro data in the U.S. First, as noted in our January 2026 Outlook , data indicates the current buildout of AI-related data centers and infrastructure is accounting for roughly half of U.S. GDP growth, i.e., while headline growth is around 2%, “Main Street” is growing about 1%. This is “fine,” but it is not particularly differentiated compared to the GDP growth seen in much of the rest of the world. In the 2010s, the U.S. economy was truly outpacing most of the world. But in the last several years, other economies have improved, while the U.S. economy has softened in sectors not exposed to the AI investment cycle. Second, because the U.S. is a large energy producer, GDP calculations positively incorporate the improving trade balance from higher-priced energy exports. However, only about 500,000 Americans work in the energy industry, while nearly 200 million people are employed in other sectors. Consequently, far more U.S. consumers have been pinched by higher energy prices than may see higher incomes from the March-to-June spike. GDP may indicate a strong macro environment, but just as Main Street growth is currently running around European levels, U.S. and European wallets were similarly impacted by the recent energy price volatility. While the U.S.-led AI-driven tech cycle is currently strong, it is important to remember that it is a cycle . There are a small number of companies spending enormous amounts of money, and most of it is flowing through the U.S. construction industry (data centers) and the global semiconductor supply chain. Two different dynamics are driving narratives and investment decisions: Leading AI models have proven to be highly functional, and therefore several companies are generating substantial – and still accelerating – revenue deploying their services. However, the AI providers have not yet proven their business models can be highly profitable. The scope of investment has led to bottlenecks in physical tech and general infrastructure, which creates usage and pricing behaviors often seen for scarce resources. Potential AI capabilities, combined with uncertain monetization dynamics, may lead to increased regulation, and consequently, it remains difficult to predict what normalized earnings might look like for the AI ecosystem. The points above highlight why investors are excited, but also why they must stay disciplined. We know the “hyperscale” companies investing in AI have not only ramped their spending at an almost unimaginable speed, but after having long been highly cash generative, in 2026, they will (in aggregate) spend nearly all their operating cash flow on capital expenditures. This year, they have also been the largest new issuers in the corporate bond market. AI Has Caused the Tech Industry’s Capital Intensity to Increase Dramatically Hyperscalers’ Aggregate Capital Expenditures Source: Bloomberg as of 5 July 2026 Yet we are unlikely to know for several years whether AI-related profits can earn attractive returns on this investment. As with all investments, scenario analysis and consideration of the asymmetry of different outcomes are essential. In hot markets, and particularly narrow markets where “FOMO” takes hold, investors should not forget the importance of downside protection. An Improvement in Market Breadth Should Be Good for Stock Pickers There is a solid case for identifying stock-specific alpha opportunities in the AI space, but there are also clear risks to painting with too broad a brush. In momentum- and narrative-driven markets, it can be difficult to remember the benefits of a genuinely diversified equity portfolio. A rare occurrence in 1H26 was narrow market breadth both inside the U.S. and elsewhere in the world. The U.S. market has narrowed considerably over the last decade as passive and levered ETFs increased correlations and sometimes created a circular reference for flows reinforcing flows, regardless of fundamentals. Only 1/3 of stocks in the S&P 500 are outperforming, the lowest share in more than 35 years. International indices have generally seen a much smaller portion of their returns coming from the very largest companies, but the AI semiconductor rally also narrowed the breadth of returns outside the U.S. Market Leadership Has Narrowed Globally, but the U.S. Remains More Concentrated U.S Index Concentration vs. International Breadth Source: Factset, as of 30 June 2026 Currently, the earnings growth is incredible for beneficiaries of this AI-related surge in spending. But other areas of the global economy, with low- or no-dependence on the AI supply chain, should not be forgotten. While global nominal GDP is growing in the mid-single digits, strong businesses operating across many sectors and regions are still expected to grow earnings at double-digit rates. Yet, for roughly equivalent growth outlooks, international stocks across sectors continue to trade at a discount to their U.S. peers (a simplified comparison is shown below between the equal-weighted indices to mitigate the effects of mega caps). International Markets Offer Comparable Growth at Lower Valuations Source: Bloomberg as of 5 July 2026 We note that although brokerages’ consensus estimates are for U.S. non-tech earnings to grow slightly faster than the rest of the world, it is worth remembering that many leading international companies have been beating consensus expectations over the last few years. But it’s not necessary to add international stocks to a portfolio simply to play the “beat-and-raise” game. Investors in international stocks can also benefit from the optionality around a weakening U.S. dollar and notably lower valuations, while being “paid to wait” with dividend yields that tend to be 2-3 percentage points higher than similar U.S. stocks. 2022 and 2025 are recent reminders that diversification can enhance absolute return, and especially risk-adjusted returns, across the cycle. In a world where inflation remains reasonably predictable (although above the levels desired by central bankers) and economic growth remains positive (even if not as high as many would wish), looking beyond the hot dots of big tech to the broad variety of truly durable companies around the world can still be additive to client portfolios. Final Thought We face continued unpredictability in the second half as markets assess elections in the U.S. and other major economies, central bank decisions, and clear resolutions to myriad geopolitical complexities. And while the impact to GDP growth from current AI spending is known, whether these AI expenditures actually generate a sufficient future return on investment remains a question that investors will need to carefully assess. With this backdrop, and given that the Main Street U.S. economy is on a more level playing field with other global economies, the sustainability of the 2Q26 melt-up in U.S. stocks is uncertain. Given the downside protection that comes from lower starting valuations and higher dividend yields, in many markets outside the U.S., it’s worthwhile for equity investors (based anywhere in the world) to consider reducing their U.S. allocations and diversifying into other geographies. Great companies in all regions continue to adapt to succeed in this changing landscape. While we remain “macro and policy aware,” we are most focused on the resilience and unique characteristics of each individual investment. We believe the most valuable service portfolio managers can provide clients isn’t predicting politics or the macro, but rather to identify relative value in the shares of businesses that don’t simply survive, but can actually thrive, during uncertain times. title: Jacobs to deliver engineering design for military installations across the US national capital region
summary: Jacobs has been selected by Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command Washington to deliver architectural and engineering services for military installations under an indefinite delivery/indefinite quantity single-award task order contract.
body_text: DALLAS – Jacobs (NYSE: J) has been selected by Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command (NAVFAC) Washington to deliver architectural and engineering services for military installations under an indefinite delivery/indefinite quantity (IDIQ) single-award task order contract. Jacobs will plan and design projects at Navy and Marine Corps installations in Washington, D.C., Maryland and Northern Virginia. The work will include new buildings, upgrades to existing facilities and improvements to infrastructure such as utilities, roads and site systems, enabling daily operations while strengthening long‑term mission performance. Jacobs Executive Vice President Susannah Kerr said: “Jacobs has extensive experience supporting the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps with military facilities that are safe, reliable and built to perform in secure environments. By improving how these installations operate and connect to essential infrastructure, this program will help bases meet current operational demands and adapt to future mission requirements. Our work with NAVFAC Washington strengthens military readiness and supports the communities where service members and civilian personnel live and work.” Ranked as No. 1 in Government Offices and No.1 in the Top 100 Pure Designers by Engineering News-Record , Jacobs delivers some of today’s most complex facilities and supporting infrastructure for federal clients and government agencies , including military bases and secure environments. Whether it’s energy, water, transportation, civil or other critical infrastructure, the company supports with environmental compliance, remediation, regeneration and program management solutions. At Jacobs, we're challenging today to reinvent tomorrow – delivering outcomes and solutions for the world’s most complex challenges. With approximately $12 billion in annual revenue and a talent force of approximately 47,000, we provide end-to-end services in advanced manufacturing, cities & places, energy, environmental, life sciences, transportation and water. From advisory and consulting, feasibility, planning, design, program and lifecycle management, we’re creating a more connected and sustainable world. See how at jacobs.com and connect with us on LinkedIn , Instagram , X and Facebook . title: Top 11 Flocksy Alternatives to Try in 2026
summary: Compare the 11 best Flocksy alternatives for 2026, with real pricing, pros and cons, and how to pick an unlimited design service that fits your team.
body_text: Key takeaways: Flocksy sells creative capacity in daily-hour blocks starting at $1,199/month, and its best rates need annual billing, with monthly plans costing roughly 30% more. On the entry tier you don't get a production coordinator or art director, and video is gated to higher plans, so the real cost of a full creative team is higher than the sticker. The best alternatives swap hour-blocks for true unlimited requests, a lower entry price, or bundled video and motion. Awesomic matches you with vetted talent in up to 24 hours and covers design, no-code, and video under one flat fee, with unlimited revisions on every plan. Flocksy's pitch is a familiar one done well: the same creative team on every brief, unlimited requests, and a flat monthly rate. Selling capacity in daily-hour blocks makes budgeting predictable, and the rollover-hours perk is genuinely useful. But the model has edges. The advertised prices assume annual billing, the entry tier skips the coordinator and art director, and if you think in "requests" rather than "hours," the block system takes some getting used to. This guide rounds up the 11 best Flocksy alternatives for 2026, with what each does well, real pricing, and how to choose. We build one of them, Awesomic, and we'll be straight about where we're the better fit and where another option wins. Every other service is described on the facts. Why look for Flocksy alternatives? Flocksy suits teams that like the dedicated-team model and can commit annually. The reasons buyers compare alternatives are usually about pricing structure and what's included: The headline rates need annual billing, and paying monthly costs noticeably more. The entry 2-hour plan has no production coordinator or art director, so lighter oversight comes only at higher tiers. Video and motion are stronger on the upper plans, so a team that leans on video may need to buy up. Thinking in daily hours instead of active requests can make it harder to compare against unlimited-request services. There's also a reliability angle worth naming. On Reddit, one buyer who evaluated unlimited-design services warned that "unlimited" plans often cap out at a couple of simple tasks a day once revisions are counted, so the effective throughput is lower than it sounds ( shared on Reddit , one user's experience). Reading the throughput terms, not just the monthly rate, matters across every service here. None of this makes Flocksy a weak choice. It means teams that want simpler unlimited-request pricing, a lower entry point, or video built into the base plan have good reasons to shop around, and the wider design subscription model now offers plenty of shapes to choose from. And the payoff for getting design right is real: McKinsey's research found the top companies on its Design Index grew revenue 32 percentage points faster than their peers over five years, so the service you pick genuinely affects results. The best Flocksy alternatives Here's how the 11 alternatives compare. Awesomic leads the table as the option we build, with its limits stated plainly. Pricing is the lowest public monthly rate for a comparable plan; ratings reflect our read of value, breadth, and reliability. Service Best for Key strengths Main limitation Pricing (from) Rating Awesomic Startups needing design, web, and video Vetted talent matched in 24h, broad scope, unlimited revisions Not the cheapest entry point $1,490/month ★★★★★ Design Pickle Managed graphics at scale Brand-trained team, fast first drafts Quote-only, no public pricing Custom ★★★★½ Kimp Bundled graphics and video Graphics + video in one fee 2–5 active requests by plan $1,397/month ★★★★ Superside Enterprise creative at scale Senior AI-native teams, huge breadth $15,000/month floor, annual term $15,000/month ★★★★ Penji Simple marketing graphics on a budget Low $499 entry, art-director oversight 1 project at a time on entry tier $499/month ★★★★½ ManyPixels Startups wanting source files and IP Full IP transfer, choose your designer No sub-$500 or free tier $699/month ★★★★ Kapa99 Fast, flat-fee parallel design Unlimited parallel tasks, free trial Output can be uneven $499/month ★★★½ Draftss Design plus development in one plan Design-to-dev scope, white label 1 active task on entry tier $490/month ★★★½ 99designs One-off logos and brand concepts Many competing concepts, fixed prices Not an ongoing subscription $249/project ★★★★ DotYeti Clear turnaround SLAs Published day-based SLAs, 3D on top tiers Only 2 parallel requests up to Summit $995/month ★★★★ Delesign A named designer at a mid-tier price Dedicated senior designer, keep work on refund Queue is ~2 hours/day, serial $599/month ★★★★ Every service below includes a screenshot, real pricing, and honest pros and cons, and each is a form of on-demand graphic design you can start this week. We begin with Awesomic. Awesomic Best for: startups that need design, web, and video handled together. Awesomic gets your design, no-code, and video work done for a fixed monthly fee, matched to vetted talent rather than sold as a block of hours. Instead of budgeting by daily-hour allotments, you brief a task and we match you with a designer from the top 0.82% of applicants in up to 24 hours. That matching model is the core difference from an hours-based service. There's no metering your allocation or worrying whether a big week eats your hours; you submit requests, get unlimited revisions, and we keep the work moving. If a designer isn't the right fit, we re-match at no cost. Our scope spans branding, UI/UX, product and web design , Webflow and Framer builds, plus video and motion, so one subscription replaces several vendors. More than 4,000 businesses have completed 20,000+ projects with us, and we hold a 4.9 rating on Google and Trustpilot. Key features: Vetted talent matched in up to 24 hours, so briefs turn into work the same day Design, no-code, and video in one subscription, not a discipline you buy up to Unlimited revisions on every plan, with no hour-block metering A dedicated project manager on the 1-to-1 tier for multi-part projects A free re-match if the fit isn't right, so quality never stalls on one person Slack integration on paid plans for fast, real-time collaboration Pricing: the Graphic Pack starts at $1,490/month (or $1,190/month billed quarterly) for part-time talent and graphic design. The All-in-one plan is $2,995/month (or $2,396/month quarterly) and adds no-code, copywriting, and QA. An AI Designer plan is $200/month, and the 1-to-1 tier with full-time dedicated talent plus a PM is custom. Monthly plans have no commitment. Pros: fast 24-hour matching, vetted top-tier talent, request-based rather than hour-metered, broad scope, unlimited revisions. Cons: not the cheapest entry point, quarterly plans carry a 3-month minimum. How to start using Awesomic: Pick a plan on our pricing page that matches your mix of design, no-code, and video. Send over a short brief with your brand, goals, and first request. Get matched with a vetted designer in up to 24 hours. Collaborate over Slack or the dashboard as work comes back. Request revisions until it's right, then download the final files. Why it's a good Flocksy alternative: it replaces hour-block budgeting with straightforward request-based work and 24-hour matching, and it bundles video without making you buy a higher tier. Final verdict: if you like the dedicated-team idea but not the hours math, Awesomic is the strongest all-round option here. Get started and get matched within a day. Design Pickle Design Pickle is a long-running creative-as-a-service platform that assigns a brand-trained team for unlimited graphic design, motion, and illustration, with production coordinators built into the model. Key features: A dedicated team trained on your brand up front, plus coordinator and art-director support Next-business-day first drafts, with most work returned in 24–48 hours Delivery in Adobe, Canva, Figma, and Google Slides with full client IP Pricing: custom and quote-only as of 2026, set on a consultation call, billed quarterly or annually. There's no public number to line up against Flocksy's. Pros: brand-trained team, coordinators included, fast stated turnaround. Cons: you must book a call to learn the price, quarterly or annual billing only. Why it's a good Flocksy alternative: it bakes coordinator oversight into the core service rather than gating it to higher tiers the way Flocksy does. Final verdict: a capable managed alternative if you're comfortable with quote-based pricing. Kimp Kimp runs unlimited graphics and video on one flat fee, with a dedicated team and the KIMP360 platform for briefing and feedback, so both media live in a single subscription. Key features: Graphics, video, or a combined plan, so you match spend to your work mix A dedicated team plus a project manager included on every tier Unlimited seats, so anyone on your team can file requests Pricing: $1,397/month for Graphics or Video and $1,697/month for Graphics + Video, with a promo halving the first four months. Budget on the list price. Pros: graphics and video bundled, dedicated team, unlimited seats. Cons: 2–5 active requests by plan, steep list price, promo-based headline rate. Why it's a good Flocksy alternative: where Flocksy gates video to its upper tiers, Kimp treats video as a first-class part of the subscription. Final verdict: the better pick if video is central to your output rather than an add-on. Superside Superside is an enterprise-grade creative subscription, fielding senior, AI-native teams across video, motion, branding, web, and presentations for large marketing organizations. Key features: Senior specialists across a broad creative range under one contract The Superspace platform with Brand Brain for AI-assisted, on-brand briefing Budget rollover for up to three months on Flex plans Pricing: from a $15,000/month minimum on a 12-month term, plus a $1,000/month software fee, with everything above the floor quoted by sales. Pros: deep senior bench, wide scope, budget rollover. Cons: $15,000/month floor, mandatory annual commitment, extra software fee. Why it's a good Flocksy alternative: it's the tier above Flocksy for teams whose volume and complexity justify enterprise budget. Final verdict: right only for enterprises replacing an agency, not lean teams. Penji Penji is a budget-friendly unlimited graphic design subscription with a dedicated remote team and art-director oversight, popular with SMBs and agencies. Key features: 120+ design services under unlimited requests and revisions 1-day delivery on the Business and Marketing tiers A white-label portal on the Agency plan for resellers Pricing: Business $499/month, Marketing & Ads $995/month, Agency $1,995/month, with quarterly and yearly discounts and a 30-day money-back guarantee. Pros: low entry price, wide scope, 30-day guarantee. Cons: 1 project at a time on the $499 tier, video gated to the top plan, no free trial. Why it's a good Flocksy alternative: it starts at a fraction of Flocksy's entry rate with no annual-billing requirement to unlock the price. Final verdict: the value pick for graphics-led teams that can work one project at a time. ManyPixels ManyPixels offers unlimited graphic, web, and motion design for a flat monthly fee, with a chosen designer and full ownership of every deliverable. Key features: Full copyright and native source files handed over on every project Next-business-day first drafts with a Slack channel to your designer Unlimited brands under one plan for agency use Pricing: Advanced $699/month ($559 annually) and Business $1,199/month ($959 annually), with a $10/month pause option. Pros: full IP and source files, choose your designer, pause option. Cons: no free tier, base tier is serial, tier naming is confusing. Why it's a good Flocksy alternative: it gives you request-based unlimited design and source-file ownership below Flocksy's entry rate. Final verdict: a reliable mid-priced option, especially if owning source files matters. Kapa99 Kapa99 is a flat-fee unlimited graphic design service that stands out for working requests in parallel rather than one at a time, with a genuine free trial. Key features: Unlimited active tasks worked in parallel, not queued singly Native Adobe and Canva file delivery on every plan A 15-day free trial with no card, plus a 30-day money-back guarantee Pricing: Async Standard $499/month (2-day delivery), Async Priority $999/month (1-day), and Dedicated Team $2,500/month (same-day). Pros: parallel task handling, real free trial, month-to-month. Cons: quality can be uneven, big jump to the top tier, no per-task pricing. Why it's a good Flocksy alternative: its parallel-task model and free trial let you test throughput cheaply before committing, unlike Flocksy's annual-leaning pricing. Final verdict: worth a trial if budget and parallel speed matter; check quality during the free window. Draftss Draftss is a subscription creative-to-dev team, starting with unlimited graphic design and scaling up to development, copy, and even PPC and SEO on higher tiers. Key features: Scope that grows from graphics to a full design-and-development team White-label delivery, NDAs, and full IP transfer on every tier A 7-day free trial with cancel-anytime terms Pricing: Graphic Team $490/month list (1 active task); Creative Team $1,190/month and Full Team $2,780/month, each also at 3 active tasks, with a new-customer promo halving the first six months. Pros: design-to-dev scope, white label, free trial. Cons: 1 active task on entry, promo-based headline rate, steep jump to Full Team. Why it's a good Flocksy alternative: if your roadmap needs code alongside creative, Draftss covers both under one plan where Flocksy stops at creative. Final verdict: best when you need development and design from a single subscription. 99designs 99designs is a design marketplace and contest platform rather than a subscription, useful when you need a one-off logo or brand identity with many concepts to choose from. Key features: Design contests that surface dozens of competing concepts in one round Fixed, published prices per category, plus 1-to-1 direct hire A money-back guarantee and full copyright transfer on the winner Pricing: logo contests start at $249 (Bronze) and rise to $1,050 (Platinum); 1-to-1 projects are negotiated per designer. Pros: many concepts fast, published prices, money-back guarantee. Cons: not an ongoing subscription, billed per project, opaque 1-to-1 rates. Why it's a good Flocksy alternative: for a single big creative moment like a rebrand, a contest can beat paying a monthly subscription you won't fully use. Final verdict: the right tool for one-off brand work, not continuous design volume. DotYeti DotYeti is an unlimited graphic design subscription with a dedicated team and clearly published, tier-based turnaround SLAs, so delivery dates are spelled out. Key features: Day-based turnaround that tightens as you move up tiers Motion, video, 3D, and light web development on higher plans A 14-day satisfaction guarantee, no long-term contract Pricing: Base $995/month, Scale $1,595/month, Summit $2,595/month, Apex Studio from $3,995/month, with a six-month prepay discount. Pros: transparent SLAs, broad higher-tier scope, no lock-in. Cons: 2 parallel requests up to Summit, high entry price, quote-heavy top tier. Why it's a good Flocksy alternative: its written SLAs remove the ambiguity of hour-block delivery estimates. Final verdict: a good fit for teams that want delivery commitments on paper. Delesign Delesign pairs you with a dedicated senior designer and a design manager who work your queue, with an unusually specific turnaround table by asset type. Key features: A named senior designer plus a design manager on your account A free designer swap if the match isn't right A 15-day money-back guarantee that lets you keep finished work Pricing: graphic design $599/month, with web development ($649/month), multimedia ($799/month), and SEO writing ($399/month) as separate tracks. Pros: dedicated senior designer, keep work after a refund, per-asset turnaround clarity. Cons: serial queue (~2 hours/day), no free trial, animation can take 7–15 days. Why it's a good Flocksy alternative: it delivers a named-designer relationship at roughly half Flocksy's entry rate. Final verdict: a solid mid-priced pick when a consistent designer beats raw parallel speed. Pros and cons of switching from Flocksy Switching brings real gains and a little friction, so weigh both. On the upside, you can drop the annual-billing requirement, start at a lower monthly rate, and choose a model that fits how you think about work, whether that's unlimited requests, parallel tasks, or bundled video. Several alternatives include a free trial, so you can test before you commit a cent. On the downside, any new team needs a short ramp to learn your brand, and you'll re-share assets and reset your feedback loop. If you rely on Flocksy's rollover hours to smooth busy weeks, check how a new service handles surges. And a cheaper plan can mean fewer parallel requests, so confirm throughput before you move. The honest read: if Flocksy's pricing structure, gated coordinator, or video tiering is a real friction, an alternative will likely serve you better. If the dedicated-team model works and you can commit annually, staying is reasonable. Our side-by-side on Awesomic versus traditional freelancers is a useful gut check on what managed delivery buys you. How much do Flocksy alternatives cost? Flocksy's entry rate of $1,199/month (annual) sits mid-pack, so several alternatives come in lower, especially the request-based subscriptions. Here's the lowest public monthly entry point for each. Service Entry plan Starting price Billing note 99designs Bronze contest $249/project Per project, not monthly Draftss Graphic Team $490/month (list) Promo halves first 6 months Penji Business $499/month 15% off quarterly, 20% yearly Kapa99 Async Standard $499/month Intro discount first 2 months Delesign Marketer Growth $599/month Month-to-month ManyPixels Advanced $699/month $559/month billed annually DotYeti Base $995/month ~10% off 6-month prepay Kimp Graphics $1,397/month Promo halves first 4 months Awesomic Graphic Pack $1,490/month $1,190/month quarterly Design Pickle Custom Quote-only Quarterly or annual Superside Flex $15,000/month Annual term + software fee The subscriptions cluster between $490 and $1,500 per month, while 99designs is priced per project for one-off work and Superside sits in a different, enterprise league. Match the billing model to your workload: steady volume favors a subscription, while a single rebrand may be cheaper as a contest. Read what each plan includes rather than the entry price alone. This flexible-spend approach mirrors a broader hiring shift, too: The CMO Survey found planned full-time marketing hiring fell from 82.5% in 2019 to 77.9% in 2025, with more work going to independent and on-demand talent. How hard is it to migrate from Flocksy? Leaving Flocksy is mostly a matter of moving context, not untangling technical lock-in. Budget a few days of prep and one project cycle to settle in. Download your finished files and source assets from Flocksy before you cancel or let the plan lapse. Assemble a brand kit: logos, fonts, color codes, tone notes, and a few examples of work you liked. Pick your new service and start with a real but low-stakes task to judge quality and turnaround. Set up your feedback channel and agree how revisions and priorities get flagged. Run one full cycle, note where drafts missed, and refine the brief for the next round. If you've been using Flocksy's hour-block system, the biggest mental shift is moving to request-based or parallel-task models, so brief a couple of typical tasks early to calibrate. A quick refresher on the graphic design process can help you write briefs a new team can act on fast. Expect a slightly slower first week or two while the new team learns your brand, then you'll be back to pace with the pricing and scope gaps closed. Common mistakes to avoid when choosing an alternative A few predictable missteps cost teams time when switching: Comparing an hour-block plan to an unlimited-request plan on price alone, without translating what each actually delivers. Taking "unlimited" at face value. Ask how many requests run at once and what a realistic daily output looks like. Missing the annual-versus-monthly gap. Some headline rates, Flocksy's included, assume annual billing. Skipping the trial. The first project reveals onboarding quality faster than any sales page. Forgetting video or web needs. If they matter, confirm they're in your plan, not a costly upgrade. Avoiding these comes down to matching the service to how your team actually works and testing before you commit. List your must-haves, then trial the two closest fits. How to choose the right Flocksy alternative for your needs The best pick depends on what pushed you to look past Flocksy. A quick way to decide: If you want the dedicated-team feel without hour-block math or an annual commitment, Awesomic fits, with request-based work and 24-hour matching. If price is the driver, Penji, Kapa99, and Draftss all start under $700/month. If you need video front and center, Kimp bundles it without a tier jump. If you want parallel throughput, Kapa99 is built for it, and if you need one-off brand work, 99designs' contest model may be cheaper than any subscription. Enterprises should look at Superside. It also helps to scan the wider market in an independent design subscription directory before shortlisting. And if you're weighing specific tools, we've compared Penji alternatives , Kimp alternatives , and Design Pickle alternatives in their own guides. Our overview of unlimited design services covers the full field. Whatever you shortlist, trial two before committing. The right Flocksy alternative closes your specific gap, whether that's simpler pricing, a lower entry point, or bundled video, not just a lower number on the page. The bottom line on switching Flocksy's hour-block pricing and annual-leaning rates are what send most teams looking, but the real reason to switch is fit. Decide whether you want request-based simplicity, parallel throughput, bundled video, or the lowest entry price, then trial your top two with a real task. Keep the one whose first drafts land closest to your brand and whose model matches how you actually plan work. Do that and you'll trade hour math for a service that just gets the work done. FAQs What is the best Flocksy alternative in 2026? It depends on your priority. For a dedicated-team feel without hour-block pricing, Awesomic is the strongest all-round pick. For the lowest price, Penji and Kapa99 start at $499/month, and for bundled video, Kimp is purpose-built. Is Flocksy's pricing monthly or annual? Flocksy's advertised tier prices, from $1,199/month for 2 daily hours, assume annual billing. Paying monthly costs roughly 30% more, which is one reason buyers compare alternatives that publish a straightforward monthly rate. Are Flocksy alternatives cheaper? Several are. Request-based subscriptions like Penji, Kapa99, Delesign, and ManyPixels start between $499 and $699 per month, below Flocksy's entry rate, though throughput and scope differ. Compare what each plan includes rather than the entry price alone. Which Flocksy alternatives include video? Kimp bundles graphics and video in one subscription, Awesomic covers video and motion alongside design and no-code, and DotYeti adds video on higher tiers. Confirm the specific plan, since some services gate video behind an upgrade. Can I try a Flocksy alternative before committing? Yes. Kapa99 offers a 15-day free trial with no card, Draftss has a 7-day trial, and several others include money-back guarantees. Use the trial window to test onboarding and quality with a real task before you switch.

title: The Ultimate Checklist for Buying Used Heavy Equipment
summary: Learn how to buy used heavy equipment with confidence. Our inspection checklist and expert guidance help you make informed decisions. Contact us today.
body_text: Buying Used Heavy Equipment Ultimate Checklist Buying used heavy equipment is a great way to expand your fleet or replace older machines. The key is knowing exactly what to inspect in the equipment before you commit. After all, you’ll need a quality piece of equipment to avoid downtime and repairs. Follow our equipment inspection checklist to make more confident purchases. What to Do Before You Inspect the Machine The physical inspection is only half the battle when buying used heavy equipment. Before you ever lay eyes on the machine, follow these steps to position yourself for success: Define your specs and job requirements: Think like a fleet manager by defining the job the machine needs to accomplish. Know your required specifications, like lift capacity, engine power, GVWR and application-specific features, before you start shopping. This prevents you from overbuying capabilities you won’t use or underbuying power you’ll desperately need. Whether you’re considering specialized vocational trucks or tracked equipment, knowing your requirements helps you focus the search and negotiate from a position of knowledge. Know how to vet the seller: You can source your used equipment from different places, whether it’s a dealer, auction or private seller. The most important thing across all three sources is the seller’s ability to provide transparent, verifiable information about a machine’s history and condition. A reputable dealer who services what they sell offers a significant advantage — they can back up claims with maintenance records performed by their own technicians. Set a realistic budget beyond the sticker price: The total cost of ownership extends well beyond the purchase price. Budget for immediate costs like transport, taxes and insurance, as well as potential near-term expenses for tires, fluids or other wear parts. Always have a contingency fund for initial repairs or maintenance. When evaluating equipment like excavators, dozers and wheel loaders, factor in the operating costs specific to each machine type. Heavy Equipment Prepurchase Inspection Checklist Follow this used heavy equipment checklist to protect your investment and choose a top-quality machine: 1. Inspect the Frame and Structure for Cracks and Wear Start with a thorough walk-around of the entire machine. Look for signs of structural stress, especially around high-load areas, as well as fresh paint that could be hiding rust or previous repairs. Inspect all welds carefully, especially around booms, cranes and mounting points. Make sure the equipment doesn’t have any cracks, as these could mean it’s been stressed beyond its design limits. Examine the chassis for any bending or twisting that suggests the equipment has been in an accident or used improperly. Any inspection you perform should meet the federal structural integrity requirements outlined by the FMCSA. 2. Evaluate the Engine, Power Train and Exhaust The engine can tell you a lot about how the machine was operated. Check for oil leaks around seals, gaskets and the oil pan. Listen closely during a cold start for any strange sounds, such as knocking, which could indicate worn bearings. Remove the oil fill cap while the engine is running and check for excessive blowby, which suggests worn piston rings or cylinder walls. Note the color of exhaust smoke, as different colors indicate specific engine problems. Blue may mean burning oil, white suggests coolant in the combustion chamber, and black points to fuel system problems. Test the transmission through all gears and note how the machine shifts under load. 3. Test the Hydraulic System for Leaks and Performance For vocational trucks and heavy equipment, a well-functioning hydraulic system is essential. Check all the hoses for brittleness, cracks, and signs of previous repairs. Look for leaks around hydraulic cylinders, pumps, and fittings. Operate the equipment under a light load to test for hydraulic drift, where a raised implement slowly lowers on its own. This indicates worn seals or valves. Hydraulic fluid levels and condition show you whether the system is in good shape. 4. Check All Cab Controls and Electrical Systems Get in the cab and test every single component. Make sure every light works, every gauge responds accurately, and every switch functions as designed. Test the PTO engagement if applicable. A faulty electrical system can be difficult and expensive to diagnose and repair, so thorough testing now will save you from trouble later on. Check the condition of wiring harnesses for signs of rodent damage or previous amateur repairs. 5. Examine the Undercarriage, Tires or Tracks For wheeled equipment, check for uneven tire wear patterns, as these usually indicate alignment or suspension issues. Measure tread depth and check for sidewall damage. For tracked equipment, examine the sprockets, idlers, and the track itself for signs of wear, cracks, and missing components. An undercarriage replacement will be a major expense, so make sure these components are in good condition to help calculate your true acquisition cost. How to Verify the Equipment’s True History Documentation is just as important as your physical inspection. Knowing how to buy used heavy equipment means understanding service records, as these will tell you the true story of how equipment was treated during its working life: Review the service history: A quality service history shows consistent, preventive maintenance rather than just reactive repairs. Look for regular fluid changes, scheduled inspections and proactive component replacements. This documentation can prove that the previous owner invested in the machine’s longevity. Equipment maintained by expert technicians will usually come with detailed records, so you can be more confident in the machine’s condition. Know the difference between high hours and hard hours: An hour meter doesn’t tell the full story about a machine’s condition. A truck with high highway miles might be in much better shape than a low-hour unit that spent its entire life in severe-duty applications. Consider engine idle time versus PTO hours. Idle hours significantly impact engine wear , so you’ll need to factor them into the used equipment valuation. A machine with an auxiliary power unit might show high hours but less actual engine stress. Confirm you’re getting a clean title with no liens: Always run a formal lien check on any equipment you’re considering purchasing. This ensures the seller has the legal right to transfer ownership and that you won’t inherit outstanding debts attached to the machine. A clean title protects your investment from future legal complications. When you partner with a reputable company like Custom Truck One Source, you can rely on our expertise to handle the verification process for you. We know what to look for in service records because we’ve maintained these machines ourselves. Find a Work-Ready Unit With Custom Truck One Source When you’re ready to invest in reliable, work-ready equipment, turn to Custom Truck One Source for a solution built on transparency and quality. Much of our inventory comes from our own rental fleet, so you get verifiable service histories maintained by our technicians. Each unit undergoes a rigorous inspection process to meet performance and compliance standards before it reaches your operation. Browse our inventory to explore used construction equipment for sale, or contact us to discuss specific models and availability for your fleet. Ready to keep your fleet moving? title: How to Set Up a Trust: A Comprehensive Guide for 2026
summary: Online and do-it-yourself options walk you through how to set up a trust. Revocable trust, irrevocable trust, living trust, or testamentary trust, all options are available to people from all economic strata.
body_text: FAQs on how to set up a trust 1. How do I transfer ownership of my house to my trust? To transfer ownership of your house to a trust, you need to create the trust and then: Draft a new deed transferring ownership to the trust. File it with the appropriate local office responsible for property records, such as the county clerk, recorder of deeds, or land records office, depending on your state or jurisdiction 2. How does the trust management and administration function? Trust management and administration involve carrying out the grantor's directives, managing assets, and distributing funds to beneficiaries. Trustees are responsible for overseeing the trust assets, ensuring the trust is conducted appropriately, monitoring expenses, accounting for and reporting on trust assets, and preparing tax and regulatory filings. Trustees receive hourly compensation for their work, while the costs tied to trust management and administration can fluctuate depending on the trust's complexity and the beneficiaries' requirements. Ongoing trust management during incapacity or after death is crucial to ensure the trust serves its intended purpose and provides financial security for your beneficiaries. 3. Can I make some legal arrangements to ensure my child graduates from college before certain other assets are distributed? Yes. When setting up a trust, you can ensure a beneficiary meets a certain age requirement before receiving assets. In this case, you could designate that all educational expenses would be paid at the university level. You can then designate that your child receive all or a portion of the assets you have set aside for the educational expenses of that individual. 4. How much money do you need to have trust? You can start a trust fund for as little as $100 in initial deposit and a few hundred dollars in fees, but if you have $100,000 or more and own real estate, then a trust might be beneficial. 5. What are the three primary types of trust? There are three primary classes of trusts: revocable trusts, irrevocable trusts, and testamentary trusts. A revocable trust can be altered or terminated during the trustor's lifetime, while an irrevocable trust cannot. Finally, a testamentary trust is created within the context of a will. 6. What is the difference between a revocable trust and an irrevocable trust? A revocable trust allows the grantor to make changes or terminate the trust. In contrast, an irrevocable trust is permanent and offers greater asset protection and potential tax benefits. 7. What are the ongoing taxes on trusts? If your trust has property that gains value, loses value, or otherwise creates income, you must pay the Internal Revenue Service taxes on that trust income on Form 1041 . When filing your state income tax returns, you'll want to check your state tax code to see if you need to file locally. 8. Can I set up an irrevocable trust for myself? Yes, you can set up an irrevocable trust for yourself. However, once it’s created, you generally give up control over the assets and can't make changes without court approval or beneficiary consent. People often use irrevocable trusts to protect assets or reduce estate taxes. 9. Can I withdraw money from a trust account? If you created a revocable trust, then yes. Only the trustee has the authority to withdraw money from a trust account, and even then, it must be done according to the trust's terms. If you’re a beneficiary, you can’t withdraw money yourself unless the trust document allows for direct access. 10. How do I access a trust fund? If you're a trust fund beneficiary, your access depends on the rules set by the grantor. Some trusts allow regular distributions, while others are tied to age milestones or specific events. Speak to the trustee to understand your rights. 11. What happens when a trust is formed? When a trust is formed, the trustee becomes responsible for managing any assets owned in the name of the Trust, and beneficiaries gain rights to distributions under the terms outlined in the trust document. 12. How to put assets in a trust? Funding a trust involves retitling property and updating account ownership. For example, to move a home into a trust, you’ll need to execute a new deed naming the trust as the property owner. For bank accounts, you’ll need to update the account title with your bank to reflect the trust’s name. This process varies slightly depending on the asset type and state laws, so it’s helpful to consult an estate attorney or financial institution. 13. Can I be both the trustee and the beneficiary of a trust? Yes, you can be both the trustee and a beneficiary, especially in a revocable trust. However, if it’s an irrevocable trust, dual roles may raise legal or tax complications, so it’s best to seek professional advice.

title: From Transition to Transformation: A Site Move That Reflects How Collaboration Drives Progress
summary: By Hardy Gaschler, Director of Operations When we began the transition of injection molding operations from Ludwigsstadt, Germany, to our site in Sonneberg, Germany, the objective was clear. The company needed to consolidate operations and improve efficiency. The reason for the move was straightforward. Continuing production in Ludwigsstadtis no longer practical. At the same time, Sonneberg has developed into experts in injection molding, making it the natural location for these operations. However, moving equipment is […]
body_text: By Hardy Gaschler, Director of Operations When we began the transition of injection molding operations from Ludwigsstadt, Germany, to our site in Sonneberg, Germany, the objective was clear. The company needed to consolidate operations and improve efficiency. The reason for the move was straightforward. Continuing production in Ludwigsstadtis no longer practical. At the same time, Sonneberg has developed into experts in injection molding, making it the natural location for these operations. However, moving equipment is only one part of the story. The project required close coordination across multiple teams, including project leadership, manufacturing engineering, and planning. Weekly alignment meetings ensured that all stakeholders had a clear understanding of progress, risks, and priorities. One of the key challenges came from legacy constraints. In the past, tools were often dedicated to individual machines. This limited flexibility and made it more difficult to respond to increasing demand. As a result, the team needed to rethink how production capacity could be managed more effectively. The transition also highlighted the importance of investment in future capability. We are introducing new tools and considering additional machines. We are recreating clean room conditions in Sonneberg to meet production requirements. Although this project is primarily local, it reflects broader themes that are common in global organizations. Decisions about production and capacity are influenced by demand, supply chain considerations, and long-term strategy. This site move demonstrates how operational change and company culture are closely connected. The team is not only executing a transition. They are learning from past limitations and improving flexibility to prepare for future growth. The result will be more than a relocation. It will be a stronger and more resilient manufacturing operation. This is the Novanta Way in action.

title: Why Marketers Need to Own Their AI Context Layer
summary: Learn how an AI governance framework helps brands own their context layer, protect strategic IP and avoid vendor-led commoditization in the AI era.
body_text: On intellectual differentiation, the co-opt economy, and why the age of AI demands marketers craft and own their contextual advantage. I'm a lifelong Bostonian and have watched avidly as the “City of Champions” raised banner after banner to the rafters; a total of 13 sporting championships in this century alone. Championship teams worked feverishly to develop (and protect) proprietary intelligence that drove their success: scouting models, draft strategies, coaching routines and playbooks. Edges fiercely protected, separating winners from losers far before game performance; the most valuable IP that any GM can create, vaulted and locked. Now imagine a front office team who has spent years researching, building, executing and measuring, only to discover their strategy is being absorbed into a shared intelligence layer used by other teams in the league. Their once distinguished competitive advantage becomes the league average nearly overnight. No GM in professional sports would tolerate that for a second. But in marketing, it's happening every day, and the mechanism is almost invisible to most teams in the field. The co-opt economy is coming for your brand I often hear from brands, “our vendor is privacy safe” or “they anonymize all of the data, so we must be fine.” Make no mistake: What I’m talking about doesn't violate your privacy policies; it won't trigger data loss prevention and is perhaps overlooked in your vendor risk assessments. It hides in terms-of-service language granting platforms broad, royalty-free rights to use, modify and reproduce your customer data (your audience behaviors, engagement signals, conversion patterns) to "improve services." What that improves is a shared model that benefits every other brand on the platform, including your competitors. Many modern marketing platforms will tout that anonymization protects individual consumer identity and security, which may be true, but it does little to protect your brand's strategic patterns, your conversion signals and your audience intelligence. These, of course, are the same signals helping your partners train systems for their benefit, and in many cases, every other client on their platform. I call this “ the co-opt solution economy ” — the extraction of brand IP through platform ingestion, often disguised as features in modern marketing, advertising and sales platforms. The co-opt economy doesn’t announce itself but for the past two decades has operated quietly, contractually and at scale. However, as we move from conventional to AI-driven marketing, the stakes become multiplicatively more dangerous for brands. The accumulated intelligence about how your brand defines intent, what loyalty means in your market, which signals matter and which are noise will now power AI. The same context that should make AI output distinctly yours may run the risk of helping your competitors. As AI agents begin making decisions, generating content and orchestrating customer journeys, owning and protecting that context becomes essential. Brands that surrender it to a vendor's shared model no longer own the advantage. They subscribe to it. The alternative is simpler, less risky and more strategic: Own your context, protect it structurally and drive true brand differentiation on your terms. The co-opt economy is coming for your brand: What winning brands will own: Context What do we mean by context or context layer? It's the manifestation of your intellectual property, vernacular and differentiating characteristics that make your organization unique: definition and discovery of "high-intent signal," what "loyalty" means in your market(s), the behaviors that predict churn, how your brand speaks and even your compliance boundaries. It's the semantic DNA of your business. The more I talk to marketing leaders, especially in regulated industries, the clearer it becomes: The context layer is emerging as one of the most strategic assets a brand can own. Naturally it stands to reason that it should never be co-opted or commoditized, but rather built, curated and connected with an ecosystem that brings their solutions to your context. Making this real, consider two banks with similar customer data, both trying to reduce attrition. “Platform Bank” relies on a vendor-defined context layer. Their platforms decide what "at-risk" means, what engagement signals matter and what timing logic to apply — amalgamated in part by other brands using their services in addition to Platform Bank’s own. It's convenient, possibly turnkey, but it’s helping them and their competitors race toward average. The intelligence powering them was derived from shared or co-opted context. “Ownership Bank” builds its own context layer. Its views are anything but generic or average. Its proprietary behavioral signature has been developed through years of experience and refinement, including how the bank defines value, loyalty and customer engagement through the lens of customer relationships. When Ownership Bank applies AI, the outputs are grounded in intelligence that is uniquely its own, consistent across their agentic horizons. Brands like Ownership Bank have the strategic latitude to interoperate LLMs, bring in new partners and adopt new capabilities on their durable context that continues to grow with every interaction and keep it protected by bringing models and partners to them. In our early era of AI experimentation this pattern is giving safe velocity and optionality to those discovering their future truths without lock-in risks as well. Scott Brinker, Analyst at chiefmartec, and Frans Riemersma, Founder Analyst at Martech Tribe, validate the importance of context beyond theory. In the “State of Martech 2026” report, Brinker and Riemersma identify context engineering as a key competency of this era; disciplined curation, structuring and delivery of the right information to AI agents. Undoubtedly the context creates value, but governance and protection are what may inform those who will gain the leadership advantage from their efforts. The macro message, that context is the differentiator, harnesses the importance of a brand’s authentic voice coming through AI as opposed to commoditized output. "Context engineering is where company knowledge becomes machine-readable and customer understanding becomes actionable. The product catalog that an AI agent can query in real time. The brand voice skills that shape its tone. The governance rules that stop it from promising something you can’t deliver." —State of Martech 2026 When you outsource that interpretive layer to a vendor's ownership, or worse, allow it to be co-opted, you don't just lose operational control. You lose brand destiny. The context layer isn't a product you buy. It's the accumulated interpretive intelligence of your organization — the semantic DNA of your business. The better way: Build the context layer you own Contrary to what some early AI explorers believe, the model isn’t the moat. The moat is context. This opportunity isn't reserved for the largest brands with the deepest engineering benches. Any organization can build and own a context layer by defining its business intelligence, governing it in its own environment and bringing models and partners to it over time; namely those who support this pattern. As Baris Gultekin, Vice President of AI at Snowflake, puts it, “Bring AI to your data, not data to AI.” The premise is simple and the same applies to context: Bring the ecosystem to you, not your data and context to the ecosystem. Whether it’s one LLM that is exceptional in creative and content generation or another that builds workflow and informs go-to-market strategy, when designed optimally the context layer is the interoperable foundation for your brand’s future. Today, that's not theoretical: Snowflake runs models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek and others inside Snowflake’s governance perimeter. Models provide tremendous utility to marketing, analytic and strategy teams today, and can become interchangeable utilities without sacrificing the right tool for each job or allowing the value to be abstracted or averaged. This approach also supports those brands that are prioritizing responsible AI. Governance policies, auditability and regulatory controls become part of the context layer itself, allowing organizations to maintain oversight while preserving flexibility. Luke Ambrosetti, Snowflake's AI Architect for Marketing & Advertisers, frames the implication this way: "Every marketer needs to become AI aware to survive. The competitive edge goes to the ones who become truly AI fluent to build and own their context layer, because that's what lets them grow and defend their brand." AI fluency is what turns data and AI from generic, interchangeable utilities into a brand-specific advantage. The models are composable; the context is the asset that compounds. Marketers who can encode their own definitions, signals, judgment, and their compliance and governance rules, build context no platform can hand them out of the box, and a responsible AI foundation no vendor can replicate. The brands that win won't be the ones with the best models. They'll be the ones with the most authentic context and the deepest self-knowledge encoded into the fabric of how they work and responsibly scale. Scaling differentiation: The resonance flywheel So what does this look like in practice? If context is the strategic asset of the AI era, how do you begin owning it? Start here. Own the definitions: Identify the path you're on today. If your customer definitions, business rules and decision logic live inside or are solely defined by a vendor platform, you have a dependency, not a strategy. Bring them into an environment you govern with intelligence definitions you create and maintain. Snowflake® Horizon Context makes this straightforward . Marketing teams can define shared business logic in plain language, no code required, and those definitions become the governed foundation that every person, tool and AI agent in your organization operates from. Demand model separability: Can you swap your model without losing your accumulated intelligence? Your intelligence should survive model changes. If switching models means losing accumulated context, you've tied your intelligence layer to a utility. Pivot to durable ownership. Bring partners to your context, composably: Organizations have traditionally sent their data into a partner's environment, their models, their governance and even resolved to their schemas, often abstracting independent nuance. Instead, bring partners and applications to your governed foundation. Your context layer protects and promotes your IP. Celebrate and prioritize partners who share your interests of protection and supported differentiation. The best partners will embrace this because it makes their products more valuable. An activation partner grounded in your context delivers results a generic tool never could, and contributes their own proprietary intelligence to enrich yours. This is composability in the AI era. Put agents to work, grounded in your contextual truth: Ground agents in your business definitions, governance and operational knowledge so every recommendation reflects your intelligence, not generic assumptions. Snowflake CoWork puts an agent in the hands of every knowledge worker in your organization and empowers them with your context. When an agent draws from the context layer your team has built, every recommendation reflects your business intelligence. When your marketing team asks an agent to identify at-risk segments, it’s your risk definition. Same context, many applications, always yours. The brands that win the AI era won't be those with the best models. They'll be those with the deepest self-knowledge encoded into systems they actually own. The choice Every era in marketing has rewarded brands (and professional sports teams!) that invested in assets they controlled. In the digital era, it was data and connection. In the privacy era, it was direct customer relationships and trust. In the AI era, it's context and composability. The simple question remains: Will you own your customer context, or relinquish its leverage to those who stand to benefit from it? Your context layer is your playbook. Own it. If you're a marketing leader ready to own your context layer, we're here to help strategize. Marketing ops and data engineering teams, we’re here to help you define and execute your context layer development in an environment you actually control. That path is more accessible than it was even six months ago. And if you're a technology provider who respects your customers' intelligence rather than absorbing it, send me your privacy policy. I want to work with you to help marketers own what’s theirs.
